topic: Robin Dunbar (1992-1995): Primate Neocortex Ratio & the ~150 Social-Group Limit
visual_mode_reason: Plotting 38 primate species' neocortex-to-rest-of-brain ratios against stable troop size and extrapolating humans to ~148 (~150) directly links prefrontal/neocortical volume to multi-party relationship tracking.

primary_case.title: Robin I. M. Dunbar's 38-genus primate neocortex-ratio regression & human ~150 group-size validation
primary_case.place: University College London (UCL) Department of Anthropology

people.name: Robin I. M. Dunbar
people.role: Evolutionary psychologist and primatologist who discovered primate troop size scales tightly with relative neocortex volume

people.name: Leslie Aiello
people.role: Paleoanthropologist who co-analyzed hominin cranial capacity trajectories and language-as-vocal-grooming scaling with Dunbar

people.role: Evolutionary biologist whose 2021 Bayesian phylogenetic re-analysis emphasized wide statistical confidence intervals around a single fixed 150 point estimate

core_facts.fact: Why do primates carry such metabolically expensive, oversized brains (~20% of resting human energy for 2% of body mass)? In 1992, UCL anthropologist Robin Dunbar tested ecological foraging theories (fruit-map range size) head-to-head against the 'Social Brain Hypothesis' across 38 primate genera.

Territory size and diet failed to explain neocortex expansion cleanly — instead, mean SOCIAL GROUP SIZE correlated remarkably strongly (r^2 ~ 0.60-0.76) with the neocortex ratio (neocortex volume divided by the rest of the brain).

Keeping track of not just 'me and you,' but third-party alliances ('who owes whom a favor across N individuals' grows combinatorially as N*(N-1)/2) acts like a steep RAM memory tax on prefrontal and temporal neocortex.
Plugging the modern human neocortex ratio (4.1:1) into that primate regression curve predicted a natural cohesive human community size of 147.8 — famously rounded to 'Dunbar's Number' of 150.

When Dunbar checked historical and ethnographic records, ~150 popped up everywhere: Neolithic farming villages (~150), Roman army maniples (~120-160), modern military rifle companies (~130-180), Hutterite self-splitting communities (splitting right at 150 so no police force is needed!), and annual Christmas-card networks (~154 people).

Inside that ~150 outer ring, human relationships nest in fractals scaled by roughly ~3x steps depending on time investment: ~5 intimate crisis support allies, ~15 sympathy close friends, ~50 good friends, ~150 meaningful personal ties, and ~500-1,500 recognizable faces/names.

Even on digital social networks with 5,000 'friends' (Gonçalves et al. 2011 Twitter study of 1.7 million users), reciprocal two-way conversation still hits a ceiling right between 100 and 200 accounts.

Methodological boundary (Lindenfors et al. 2021): Bayesian phylogenetic regressions produce wide 95% confidence bands around point extrapolations and human institutions (laws, org charts) stretch large-scale cooperation into millions — yet individual reciprocal relationship maintenance remains constrained by both cognitive tracking AND a 24-hour social-time budget.

Across Dunbar's 1992 and 1995 comparative primate regressions, group of 150 members entails N*(N-1)/2 = 11,175 pairwise ties, while human social time concentrates roughly 40% of contact inside the innermost 5-person support clique.

wow_facts.fact: Plug the size of the human neocortex into an equation built strictly from monkey and ape brains — and out pops 147.8, the exact size of Neolithic villages, Hutterite communes, and modern army companies.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Biology quietly shaped human org charts for ten thousand years.

wow_facts.fact: Hutterite farming communities in North America have a centuries-old rule: the day a settlement grows past 150 people, they split into two villages — because past 150, peer reputation stops working and formal bureaucracy has to take over.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Peer trust fits inside one neocortical address book.

wow_facts.fact: Even when people collect 4,000 followers online, big-data analyses of 1.7 million social-media users proved active two-way conversations STILL hit a wall around 100 to 200 people.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Silicon Valley servers upgraded storage, not your prefrontal cortex.

wow_facts.fact: Forty percent of your total weekly social time goes to just your inner circle of FIVE people — and another twenty percent to the next ten.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Close friendship runs on an unforgiving clock-hour budget.

misconceptions.myth: Your brain explodes if you memorize a 151st person's name.
misconceptions.truth: Humans recognize ~1,500 faces and names easily; ~150 (broadly ~100-250) reflects active, reciprocal 'know how they fit into the web' relationships.

misconceptions.myth: Social media abolished Dunbar's limit so everyone now has 2,000 real friends.
misconceptions.truth: Likes are cheap broadcasts, not reciprocal ties; real mutual support circles stayed stuck near ~5 intimate and ~150 active ties online.

misconceptions.myth: 147.8 is a laser-exact biological constant for every single person on Earth.
misconceptions.truth: Introversion/extraversion, social time, and Lindenfors's statistical confidence bands span roughly 100 to 250 across individuals.

misconceptions.myth: Big brains evolved mainly to find ripe fruit trees.
misconceptions.truth: In Dunbar's 1992 multi-species comparison, social complexity outpredicted home-range fruit mapping as the primary neocortical driver.

everyday_hooks: Scrolling past 1,200 online connections when moving apartments and realizing there are roughly FIVE people you could actually call to carry a sofa.
Feeling an agile 80-person startup suddenly need HR handbooks and org charts the month headcount crosses ~150.
Investing real weekly dinner/walk hours into your inner 5 and 15 circles instead of spreading paper-thin across 800 acquaintances.
Splitting giant conference-hall teams into autonomous <150 'tribes' or <15 squads.
